rows.stem: During dehydration of alcohol to alkene by heating with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), the initiation step is :
rows.solution:
The initiation step is PROTONATION OF THE ALCOHOL.

The hydroxyl group is a poor leaving group and will not depart on its own. The acid's first act is to give the oxygen a proton, which converts \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{O}H_2}\) — and water IS an excellent leaving group:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Everything else in the options comes later. Water leaves in the second step, and that step is the slow, rate-determining one; the carbocation is what it leaves behind; and the ester is a side product of a different route altogether. The question asks which comes FIRST.

rows.stem: Which reagents are required for one step conversion of Chlorobenzene to Diphenyl ?
rows.solution:
The reagents are CHLOROBENZENE, SODIUM AND DRY ETHER — the Fittig reaction.

Sodium in dry ether couples two ARYL halides to one another, joining the two rings directly, so two molecules of chlorobenzene give diphenyl:
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}C_6H_5} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

This is the aryl-aryl member of the family. Coupling an aryl halide with an ALKYL halide the same way is Wurtz-Fittig, and coupling two alkyl halides is the plain Wurtz reaction.

The Friedel-Crafts option cannot work here, because the ring being attacked would have to donate to a carbon, and an aryl halide is not an electrophile of that kind.

rows.stem: Which of the following complexes show linkage isomerism ?
rows.solution:
The complex that shows linkage isomerism is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\).

Linkage isomerism needs an AMBIDENTATE ligand — one with two different donor atoms, of which it uses one at a time. The nitrite ion is the classic case: it may attach through its NITROGEN, giving the nitro form \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\), or through an OXYGEN, giving the nitrito form written here. The two are different compounds with different colours.

None of the others has such a ligand. Ammonia donates only through nitrogen, water and chloride only through the one atom they have to offer.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals has the highest melting point ?
rows.solution:
CHROMIUM has the highest melting point of the four.

Melting point in the transition series tracks the strength of the metallic bonding, which in turn tracks how many UNPAIRED d electrons are available to take part in it. Chromium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\) — six unpaired electrons, the most any element in the first series has — so its interatomic bonding is the strongest and it melts at about 2130 K.

The other three are all weaker. Scandium has only one d electron; manganese, though also half-filled at \(3d^5 4s^2\), has an unusual crystal structure that weakens its bonding; and zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\), with a full d subshell that contributes nothing at all — which is why zinc melts at a mere 693 K.

rows.stem: The reagent that can be used to convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzonitrile is :
rows.solution:
The reagent is COPPER(I) CYANIDE, CuCN — the Sandmeyer reaction.

Copper(I) cyanide replaces the diazonium group by a cyanide group, nitrogen leaving as a gas:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{CuCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5CN} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CuCl}\)

Silver cyanide is the trap, and it is a real distinction rather than an invented one: with silver cyanide the cyanide ion attaches through its NITROGEN instead, and the product is phenyl ISOcyanide, not benzonitrile. Copper(I) chloride in acid would give chlorobenzene, and methyl cyanide is a solvent here, not a cyanide source.

rows.stem: The strongest base in aqueous solution among the following amines is :
rows.solution:
DIETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), is the strongest base in aqueous solution.

Three things decide basicity in water, and they do not all point the same way. Alkyl groups RELEASE electron density onto the nitrogen, making its lone pair more available, which favours the tertiary amine. But the cation formed on protonation must also be STABILISED BY THE WATER around it through hydrogen bonding, and that requires hydrogens on the nitrogen — the tertiary amine's cation has only one, and its three ethyl groups crowd the water away besides.

The secondary amine is the compromise that wins: two alkyl groups pushing electrons in, and still one hydrogen left for solvation. In aqueous solution the observed order for ethylamines is therefore secondary, then primary, then tertiary.

Aniline is far weaker than any of them, its lone pair being delocalised into the benzene ring and so not freely available at all.

Note the qualification in the question. In the GAS PHASE, where there is no solvent to stabilise anything, the order is simply tertiary, secondary, primary — which is what makes "in aqueous solution" the load-bearing phrase here.

rows.stem: On mixing 30 mL of acetone with 20 mL of chloroform, the total volume of solution is :
rows.solution:
The total volume is LESS THAN 50 mL.

Acetone and chloroform form a solution with a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law. Neither liquid hydrogen bonds to itself, but mixing them creates a NEW hydrogen bond: the chloroform hydrogen, made acidic by the three chlorines pulling on it, bonds to the lone pair on the acetone oxygen.

The unlike molecules therefore attract one another MORE strongly than the like molecules did. Stronger attraction pulls them closer together, so the volume of mixing is negative and the solution occupies less than the 50 mL of liquid that went in.

The same fact shows up in two other ways: mixing releases heat, and the vapour pressure is lower than Raoult's law predicts.

rows.stem: We cannot measure the resistance of an ionic solution using DC because :

options.label: A
options.text: it changes the composition of the solution.

options.label: B
options.text: it can cause sparks and shocks.

options.label: C
options.text: it does not affect the composition of the solution.

options.label: D
options.text: it converts electrolytic cell to galvanic cell.

rows.solution:
Because DIRECT CURRENT CHANGES THE COMPOSITION OF THE SOLUTION.

A steady current in one direction electrolyses the solution: ions are discharged at the electrodes and products accumulate there. The concentration is then no longer what it was when the measurement started, and the electrode surfaces become polarised by the layer of product sitting on them — so the resistance being read is not the resistance of the solution that was put in.

Alternating current avoids both problems. The direction reverses hundreds of times a second, so whatever is deposited in one half cycle is taken back in the next, no net electrolysis occurs and the composition is preserved.

rows.stem: The primary and secondary valences of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\) respectively are :
rows.solution:
The primary valence is 3 and the secondary valence is 6.

The PRIMARY valence is satisfied by the ions outside the coordination sphere, and it equals what we now call the oxidation state. Here there are THREE chloride ions outside the brackets, so the primary valence is 3 — and cobalt is in the \(+3\) state, the three ethane-1,2-diamine ligands being neutral.

The SECONDARY valence is the coordination number: the count of DONOR ATOMS bonded directly to the metal. Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE, binding through both its nitrogens, so three of them supply \(3 \times 2 = 6\) donor atoms and the secondary valence is 6.

The trap is to count three ligand MOLECULES and answer 3. Coordination number counts donor atoms, never ligands.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: In the Arrhenius equation \(\mathrm{k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}}\), ‘A’ represents :
rows.solution:
In the Arrhenius equation, \(A\) is the FREQUENCY FACTOR, also called the pre-exponential factor.

It measures how often the reactant molecules collide with the right ORIENTATION — the total collision frequency scaled by the fraction of collisions that are properly aligned. It has the same units as the rate constant itself.

The exponential term is what the other options describe. \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) is the FRACTION of collisions carrying at least the activation energy, and \(E_a\) itself is the energy barrier. The product of the two, \(A \times e^{-E_a/RT}\), is the rate constant: collisions often enough, aligned rightly, AND energetic enough.

rows.stem: \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose differ from each other with respect to the :
rows.solution:
They differ in the CONFIGURATION AT THE \(\mathrm{C_1}\) CARBON.

When glucose closes into its ring, the aldehyde carbon \(\mathrm{C_1}\) becomes a new stereocentre — it now carries four different groups where it had a double bond before. The new hydroxyl can end up on either side of the ring, and the two products are called ANOMERS: \(\alpha\) with that hydroxyl below the plane, \(\beta\) with it above.

\(\mathrm{C_1}\) is therefore known as the anomeric carbon, and everything else about the two molecules is identical — same ring size, same number of hydroxyl groups, same configuration at \(\mathrm{C_2}\) through \(\mathrm{C_5}\). In solution the two interconvert through the open-chain form, which is what mutarotation is.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.
Reason (R) : Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Actinoid contraction IS greater from one element to the next than lanthanoid contraction, and actinoids DO show a wide range of oxidation states.

But the causes are different things. The contraction is steeper because the \(5f\) orbitals shield the nuclear charge even more POORLY than the \(4f\) orbitals do — they are more diffuse and reach further out — so each added proton pulls the outer electrons in harder. The wide range of oxidation states comes from the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lying close in energy.

Both statements trace back to the nature of the \(5f\) orbitals, but neither follows from the other.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Molecularity of reaction is determined experimentally.
Reason (R) : Molecularity is applicable only for an elementary reaction and not for a complex reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Molecularity is NOT determined experimentally — that is the defining property of ORDER, and confusing the two is exactly what this question tests. Molecularity is a theoretical count: the number of species that must collide in an elementary step, read off the proposed mechanism rather than measured in a flask.

The Reason is correct. Molecularity is defined only for an elementary reaction, because only there is there a single collision to count; a complex reaction is a sequence of steps and has no one molecularity at all.

Two consequences follow from the same distinction. Order may be zero or fractional, since it is measured; molecularity must be a whole number of at least 1, since it counts colliding species.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Boiling point of \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) is lower than that of \(\mathrm{n\text{-}C_4H_9NH_2}\).
Reason (R) : Hydrogen bonding is much more extensive in \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) as compared to \(\mathrm{n\text{-}C_4H_9NH_2}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Diethylamine does boil lower than butan-1-amine — about 329 K against about 351 K — even though the two have the same molecular formula and nearly the same mass. So far the Assertion holds.

But the Reason has the hydrogen bonding the wrong way round. Butan-1-amine is a PRIMARY amine with TWO hydrogens on its nitrogen; diethylamine is SECONDARY and has only ONE. Hydrogen bonding is therefore more extensive in the PRIMARY amine, not in diethylamine.

And that is precisely why the Assertion is true: fewer hydrogen bonds to break means less energy needed to separate the molecules, so diethylamine is the lower boiling of the two. The Reason, corrected, would have explained the Assertion; as written it contradicts it.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The bond angle C – O – C in ethers is slightly greater than tetrahedral angle.
Reason (R) : This is because of the repulsive interaction between the two bulky alkyl groups.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The oxygen of an ether is \(sp^3\) hybridised, so on hybridisation alone the \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) angle should be the tetrahedral \(109{\cdot}5^{\circ}\). It is measured at about \(111{\cdot}7^{\circ}\) in dimethyl ether — slightly greater, as the Assertion says.

The widening is caused by the two ALKYL groups. They are bulkier than the hydrogen atoms of water, and their mutual repulsion pushes them apart, opening the angle between them.

The contrast with water makes the point: in water the angle is \(104{\cdot}5^{\circ}\), NARROWER than tetrahedral, because there the two lone pairs dominate and squeeze the bonds together. Replacing both hydrogens by alkyl groups reverses which effect wins.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Define osmotic pressure. Why is measurement of osmotic pressure method preferred for the determination of molar masses of macromolecules such as proteins and polymers ?
rows.solution:
OSMOTIC PRESSURE is the excess pressure that must be applied on the SOLUTION side of a semipermeable membrane to just STOP osmosis — that is, to stop the net flow of solvent into the solution. For a dilute solution it is given by
\(\Pi = CRT\)
where \(C\) is the molar concentration of the solute.

Why it is preferred for MACROMOLECULES. A macromolecule has an enormous molar mass, so even a substantial mass of protein or polymer dissolves to give very few moles, and every colligative property is correspondingly tiny. The depression in freezing point or the elevation in boiling point for such a solution would be a few thousandths of a degree — below what a thermometer can read reliably.

Osmotic pressure is the exception, on three counts. Its MAGNITUDE is large and easily measured even for a very dilute solution. It is measured at ROOM TEMPERATURE, so the protein is not heated and does not denature, which the boiling point method would risk. And it uses MOLARITY rather than molality, which is the concentration a laboratory can prepare directly.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of product(s) in each of the following reactions :

(a) 1-Ethyl-2-nitrobenzene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2},\ \text{heat}}\) ?

(b) Chlorobenzene \(+\ \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{Anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}}\) ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both reactants are PRINTED AS DRAWINGS, read at 2.4x on my own page: (a) a skeletal benzene ring bearing CH2-CH3 and NO2 on ADJACENT ring carbons (ortho), (b) a skeletal benzene ring bearing Cl. Named here as 1-Ethyl-2-nitrobenzene and Chlorobenzene, which is a lossless reading and does not state the answer (the answer is the PRODUCT of benzylic bromination / Friedel-Crafts acylation), so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Bromine with HEAT and no catalyst attacks the SIDE CHAIN, not the ring — these are free radical conditions, and a bromine radical abstracts the hydrogen it can take most easily.

That is the BENZYLIC hydrogen, the one on the carbon attached to the ring, because the radical left behind is delocalised into the ring. Of the ethyl group's two carbons, only the first is benzylic.

Product: 1-(1-bromoethyl)-2-nitrobenzene — the ring keeping its nitro group, with the side chain now \(-\mathrm{CH(Br)CH_3}\).

Had the conditions instead been bromine with iron in the dark, the substitution would have been on the RING.

(b) Chlorobenzene with ethanoyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride is a Friedel-Crafts ACYLATION. The chlorine on the ring is deactivating — it withdraws electron density inductively — but it is ORTHO, PARA DIRECTING, because its lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance and that raises the density at those two positions.

Products: 1-(2-chlorophenyl)ethanone and 1-(4-chlorophenyl)ethanone — the ortho and para chloroacetophenones, with the PARA isomer predominating because the ortho position is crowded by the chlorine already there.

rows.stem:
How can you obtain the following ?

(a) Aniline from ammonium benzoate

(b) Benzene diazonium chloride from nitrobenzene

(c) 2,4,6-tribromoaniline from aniline
rows.solution:
(a) ANILINE FROM AMMONIUM BENZOATE, in two steps. Heating an ammonium carboxylate drives off water and leaves the AMIDE; Hofmann bromamide degradation then converts the amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER, which is how the seven-carbon salt becomes six-carbon aniline:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COONH_4} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)

(b) BENZENEDIAZONIUM CHLORIDE FROM NITROBENZENE, also in two steps. Tin and hydrochloric acid reduce the nitro group to an amino group, and nitrous acid generated in situ then diazotises it. The low temperature is essential — above about 278 K the diazonium salt decomposes to phenol:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\)

(c) 2,4,6-TRIBROMOANILINE FROM ANILINE, in a single step with bromine water. A white precipitate forms at once:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3NH_2} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

All three positions are substituted together and no catalyst is needed, because the amino group is so strongly activating — its lone pair is fed into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions. Stopping at the monobromo stage requires the amino group to be acetylated first.
